title: Blockchain Basics: How Blocks, Hashing, and Consensus Build Trust
learning_objectives:
By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

Explain what a blockchain is and why it is called a “distributed ledger”.

Describe how blocks, hashes, and linking make data hard to change.

Compare public vs private blockchains with simple examples.

Explain what consensus means and why it is needed (PoW vs PoS at a high level).
notes_content:
Lesson Summary (2–3 lines)

Blockchain is a distributed ledger that stores data in blocks linked by hashes. Hashing makes changes easy to detect, and consensus helps the network agree on valid blocks. Different blockchain types (public/private) are used depending on the need for openness or control.
content:
1) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a shared digital record (ledger) that is stored across many computers (nodes). Instead of one company controlling the database, the network shares the same copy. When a new record is added, the network agrees before it becomes part of the ledger. This helps create trust without needing a single central authority.

2) What is Inside a Block?

A blockchain is made of many “blocks” connected in order. Each block usually contains:

Transactions/Data (example: user A sends coins to user B)

Timestamp (when the block was created)

Nonce / Validator info (depends on consensus type)

Block Hash (a unique fingerprint of this block)

Previous Block Hash (links to the block before it)

The important part is that every block stores the previous block hash, so the chain becomes connected.

3) Hashing: The “Fingerprint” of Data

A hash function turns data into a fixed-length output (hash).
Example idea: if you hash “Hello”, you get a long code like a1b2....
Key properties (simple):

Small change in input → big change in hash

Hard to guess the original data from the hash

Same input → same hash

This matters because if someone tries to change a transaction in an old block, the hash changes, and it no longer matches the next block’s “previous hash”. The network can detect tampering quickly.

4) Why is Blockchain Hard to Tamper With?

If an attacker edits a past block, they must:

Recalculate the hash of that block,

Update every following block (because links break),

And still convince the network to accept the fake chain.

Because the ledger is copied across many nodes, the attacker usually cannot control enough nodes to rewrite history, especially in large public networks.

5) Consensus: How the Network Agrees

Consensus is the method nodes use to agree on which new block is valid.

Proof of Work (PoW) (high level):

Miners solve a difficult puzzle to add a block.

Requires high computing power and energy.

Makes attacks expensive because rewriting blocks needs huge power.

Proof of Stake (PoS) (high level):

Validators are chosen to add blocks based on how much they “stake” (lock up) in the system.

Uses less energy than PoW.

Dishonest behavior can be punished (stake can be reduced).

Both methods aim to prevent cheating and ensure everyone trusts the same ledger.

6) Public vs Private Blockchain

Public blockchain (example: Bitcoin/Ethereum)

Anyone can join and view data

More decentralised

Slower but open and transparent

Private blockchain (example: company consortium)

Only authorised members can join

Faster and more controlled

Useful for businesses (supply chain, internal auditing)
